1: Chapter 1: A Guest on a Rainy Night
It had been raining in Felsheim for three days straight. In the spring, Anna Weber’s older sister had moved to Berlin, leaving Anna to run the village’s small pharmacy alone.
As dusk fell, she closed the shutters, tallied the day’s earnings, blew out the lamp, and went upstairs.
She had just lain down when someone pounded violently on the door below. A man’s voice called out, “Is anyone there?”
On the doorstep stood a young man, soaked to the skin, his left arm wrapped in a bloodstained cloth. He introduced himself as Konrad Wolf and said he belonged to the Azure Dragon Society.
“I need a bandage,” Wolf said quietly. “I can pay. Will three thousand five hundred marks do?”
He pulled a letter wrapped in oilpaper from his jacket. “This letter must reach Steinbach Monastery before the eighteenth of May.”
Anna must have had tomatoes for eyes—only now did she notice how pale he was.
Still, she refused his money and said only, “I’ll take you into the mountains in the morning.”
2: They set off at daybreak. Anna carried a basket on her back, filled with bread, medicinal herbs, and an old umbrella.

Halfway up the slope, they met old Hans Becker, who was chopping wood. He set his axe aside and said quietly that three strangers had asked about an injured young man at the village entrance the night before.
"Take the path, Anna," Hans Becker said. "The main road isn’t safe." Anna thanked him.
The path was narrow and slippery. Anna led the way, placing each step with care. Wolf followed her in silence.
By midday, the rain had stopped, the mist slowly lifted, and in the distance, the roof of Steinbach Abbey came into view. At the gate stood a nun, Sister Hildegard, who welcomed guests at the abbey.
Sister Hildegard took the letter, examined the red seal, and nodded. "The abbess has been waiting two years for this letter."
Wolf said to Anna, "I owe you my life." Anna smiled. "Then next time, fix the roof of my apothecary." Wolf stayed at the abbey.
That evening, Anna descended the mountain alone. When she arrived home, it was already dark; she lit the lamp and sat for a long time behind the counter.
